summary: The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) can be extended, but it did not describe how extensions are managed. This informational document describes a procedure for registering and managing EPP extensions.

plainLanguage.summary: EPP is used to manage things like domain names, and people add new features to it. This sets up a list so everyone can find and keep track of the add-ons.

questions: how to register an epp extension
what is the epp extension registry
can epp extensions be deleted from the registry
subtitle: How to register and manage extensions to the Extensible Provisioning Protocol.

tldr.problem: The Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) was designed to be extended with new features as needed, but there was no formal process to manage, coordinate, or track these extensions. This led to multiple different extensions being developed for the same purpose, making it difficult for clients to support all options and reducing interoperability.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7451 creates an IANA registry with standardized registration procedures, designated expert review, and required information fields (extension name, specification, registrant contact, applicable TLDs, status, and notes) for all EPP extensions. New extensions must meet specification requirements and undergo expert evaluation to ensure architectural soundness.
tldr.outcome: A public registry now tracks all registered EPP extensions, reducing duplication and improving coordination between registry operators and extension developers. The registry helps prevent conflicting or redundant extensions and provides transparency about what extensions are available.

facts.label: Entry deletion
facts.value: Not allowed; entries marked Inactive only

today: RFC 7451 established the EPP Extension Registry at IANA and is still the authoritative reference for how EPP extensions are registered and managed. The registry continues to accept new extensions according to the procedures described in this RFC.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) is a protocol used by domain name registries to manage domain registration, including tasks like creating, updating, and deleting domain names. The protocol was designed from the start to be extended with new features using a built-in extension mechanism. However, EPP specifications (RFC 5730 and RFC 3735) did not describe how to manage these extensions or coordinate their development.

In practice, this led to a situation where different registry operators developed different extensions to solve similar problems, such as Value Added Tax (VAT) information provisioning. Registrar clients then had to support multiple competing extensions that accomplished the same goal, reducing interoperability and making client implementation more complex. RFC 7451 solves this by creating an IANA registry that coordinates and tracks EPP extensions, helping to reduce duplication and improve the overall ecosystem.
sections.plainLanguage: EPP is a system domain registries use to manage domain names. It was built to be extended with new features, but without a central list of what extensions exist, people kept inventing the same thing in different ways.

sections.title: Extension Specifications and Requirements
sections.content:
The registry uses the "Specification Required" policy from RFC 5226. This means any extension submission must include a complete English-language specification, and a designated expert must review the specification before it is accepted.

Extensions are evaluated for architectural soundness using the guidelines in RFC 3735, including security and privacy considerations. The designated expert review explicitly considers the privacy impact of proposed extensions and ensures privacy considerations are fully documented. Extensions that have already been implemented and deployed by at least one registry/registrar pair receive a more permissive review, since they have proven interoperability. Extensions that have not been deployed receive stricter evaluation to reduce functional duplication. If a proposed extension closely resembles an existing registered extension, the applicant is informed of the existing extension and asked to reconsider, though duplication alone is not a reason for rejection if all other requirements are met. If the extension specification is an IETF Standards Track document, the designated expert review is waived.
sections.plainLanguage: Before an extension gets registered, an expert reviews it to make sure it is well designed, it does not duplicate existing extensions too much, and it respects privacy.

sections.title: Registration and Management Procedures
sections.content:
Extension authors submit a standardized registration form to IANA that includes required information fields: Name of Extension (the specification title), Document Status (Standards Track, Informational, etc.), Reference (RFC number or URL to the specification), Registrant Name and Email Address (contact for managing the entry), TLDs (which top-level domains the extension applies to, or "Any" if domain-agnostic), IPR Disclosure (pointer to any Intellectual Property Rights documentation), Status (Active or Inactive), and Notes (optional additional information).

The form is sent to IANA via email to iana@iana.org with a subject line indicating "INSERT" for new entries or "MODIFY" for updates to existing entries. Upon receipt, IANA initiates review by the designated expert(s), who evaluate the request in consultation with the eppext mailing list. Issues discovered during evaluation can be corrected by the registrant until the expert makes an explicit decision to accept or reject the request. Registry entries can change state from Active to Inactive and back, for example if an extension becomes undeployed or its specification becomes unavailable. However, entries can never be deleted from the registry—only marked as Inactive.
sections.plainLanguage: To register an extension, you fill out a form with information about it and send it to IANA. An expert checks it, and if it passes, it goes in the registry.

sections.title: The IANA Registry
sections.content:
IANA created the "Extensions for the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP)" registry with a dedicated section on IANA's protocol listings. The registry includes the required information fields, the review process (Specification Required), and the reference (this document). The registry is public and provides a centralized, authoritative list of all registered EPP extensions.

RFC 7451 established initial registry entries for four existing EPP extensions: the Domain Registry Grace Period Mapping (RFC 3915), the E.164 Number Mapping (RFC 4114), the ENUM Validation Information Mapping (RFC 5076), and the Domain Name System (DNS) Security Extensions Mapping (RFC 5910). All of these initial entries were Standards Track documents, so they were registered without requiring designated expert review. New extensions submitted after the creation of this registry must go through the normal designated expert review process.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA has now published a list of registered EPP extensions that everyone can see. Four extensions were already in use, so they were added first.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
RFC 7451 introduces no new security vulnerabilities to EPP itself. However, all extensions must be evaluated in accordance with the Security Considerations of RFC 3735. The designated expert review process explicitly requires evaluation of privacy consequences and ensures that any privacy considerations are fully documented in the extension specifications.

Since EPP is used to manage sensitive registration information and control access to domain names, extension developers must carefully consider how their extensions handle authentication, authorization, data integrity, confidentiality, and auditability. The registry process ensures these considerations are reviewed before extensions are registered, reducing the risk that poorly designed extensions compromise the security of the domain registration ecosystem.
sections.plainLanguage: Extensions to EPP might affect security and privacy, so the expert review makes sure any new extension is safe to use.
